definitions.def: relating to the sense of smell
the place or thing from which something comes
to recognize or correctly name something
to say what something is like in words
the gradual process by which living things change over time

grammar_choice.en_template: Talking about what something smells like {{1:is/are}} the most basic way of {{2:talking/to talk}} about our olfactory experience, and even this most basic way of talking about smells {{3:is/being}} challenging.
grammar_choice.ko_full: 무언가가 어떤 냄새가 나는지 이야기하는 것은 우리의 후각 경험에 대해 이야기하는 가장 기본적인 방법인데, 이 가장 기본적인 방법조차도 어렵다.
explain: and 뒤 주어 'this most basic way'에 대한 정상 동사 → is.

grammar_choice.en_template: There {{1:are/is}} no words in the English language to describe smells in the same way in {{2:which/that}} "blue" or "green" describe colors.
grammar_choice.ko_full: 영어에는 "파랑"이나 "초록"이 색을 묘사하는 것과 같은 방식으로 냄새를 묘사하는 단어가 없다.
explain: in the same way in which ~ — 전치사 + 관계대명사 which.

grammar_choice.en_template: Instead, to talk about {{1:how/what}} something smells, we talk about the source of the {{2:odor/odors}}.
grammar_choice.ko_full: 대신, 무언가가 어떤 냄새가 나는지 이야기하기 위해, 우리는 그 냄새의 출처에 대해 이야기한다.
explain: smells 뒤 보어 자리 없음 → 방법을 묻는 간접의문문 how.
the source of the + 단수 명사 odor (앞서 언급된 그 냄새).

grammar_choice.ko_full: 어떤 것은 "꽃 같은", "과일 같은", 또는 "생선 같은" 냄새가 난다.

grammar_choice.en_template: Furthermore, even the most familiar odors are difficult {{1:to identify/identifying}} when they are not {{2:experienced/experiencing}} in their usual context.
grammar_choice.ko_full: 더욱이, 가장 익숙한 냄새조차도 평소의 맥락에서 경험되지 않으면 식별하기 어렵다.

grammar_choice.en_template: In one experiment the majority of participants {{1:was/were}} unable {{2:to name/naming}} very common odors like beer, urine, roses, or motor oil.

grammar_choice.en_template: Obviously, even those {{1:who/which}} couldn't name any of these odors {{2:would/would have}} drink the beer but not the urine or the motor oil.
grammar_choice.ko_full: 분명히, 이 냄새들 중 어느 것의 이름도 대지 못한 사람들조차 맥주는 마시되 소변이나 엔진 오일은 마시지 않을 것이다.

jumble.answer: Talking about what something smells like is the most basic way of talking about our olfactory experience, and even this most basic way of talking about smells is challenging.
There are no words in the English language to describe smells in the same way in which "blue" or "green" describe colors.
Instead, to talk about how something smells, we talk about the source of the odor.
Furthermore, even the most familiar odors are difficult to identify when they are not experienced in their usual context.
In one experiment the majority of participants was unable to name very common odors like beer, urine, roses, or motor oil.
Obviously, even those who couldn't name any of these odors would drink the beer but not the urine or the motor oil.
This is how evolution has shaped our brain: We respond to odors correctly in many different ways, but we are not well-equipped to talk about them.
